title: A winter density index improves same-year North Pacific oxygen estimates but gives no clear forecast gain beyond trend
abstract: We tested whether winter density changes off a fixed temperature-salinity relation predict later oxygen on sigma0 26.5 at 36-46 N, 160 E-180. Published annual aggregates were tested with expanding time splits and winter predictors at zero, one, three and five years before the target. Same-year density improves a time-trend estimate: RMSE falls from 13.76 to 12.00 umol/kg in 36 test years. One-year RMSE changes from 12.87 to 12.77, with no clear paired gain. Three- and five-year errors rise. Density improves a one-year oxygen-history model, but this gain vanishes when a trend is included. Ship-only surface data give no gain beyond trend at positive horizons. A three-cruise target rule leaves too few pairs for forecast fits. The last supported oxygen target is 2021, although the source series ends in 2025. These tests distinguish a same-year link from added forecast value. They do not reject the ventilation mechanism. Sparse cruises, fixed retrospective estimates and conditional intervals limit the result. Code, frozen aggregates, predictions and an arithmetic audit are included.

display.caption: Retrospective oxygen tests on sigma0 26.5. The middle panel compares density plus oxygen history with oxygen history alone, without trend. Intervals use five-year calendar blocks.

citations.reason: Surface aggregates and the same-year oxygen link; we test positive forecast horizons.
